Templates: template.template.html — the schema vocabulary

Purpose: documents the required/pattern/enum attribute vocabulary that turns an existing <template id="…"> skeleton into a machine-readable schema, and hosts the one generic validator function that reads it
Not a node type: unlike knowledge.template.html or spec.template.html, this file declares no <template id="…"> of its own and nothing conforms to it via data-conforms-to — there are only ever a handful of *.template.html files, hand-authored, never mixed, so the .template.html filename suffix is already sufficient signal that a file follows this convention. Nothing here needs crawler enforcement.
Sibling of: knowledge.template.html, spec.template.html

The vocabulary

Every type's <template id="…"> already contains one empty placeholder element per field, for documentation/copy-paste. Three optional attributes on those placeholders turn that skeleton into a schema, without adding any new wrapper elements:

  • required — boolean attribute (no value). The field must be present with non-empty text. Absent entirely, or present but only whitespace, both fail the same way: "missing or empty".
  • pattern — a JS regular expression source, tested against the field's trimmed text content.
  • enum — a whitespace-separated list of the only exact values the field's trimmed text may take.

A field with none of the three is optional and free-form: any content is allowed, or the field may be omitted entirely — but if it's present at all, it still can't be empty (present-but-whitespace-only is always rejected, required or not, with "present but empty — omit it instead"). The full set of field tags declared inside a type's <template> is also its allowed set: any same-family field on a real instance that isn't among them is rejected as unexpected. 

<template id="knowledge-goal">
  <knowledge-goal>
    <knowledge-title required></knowledge-title>
    <knowledge-confidence required pattern="^(0|[1-9][0-9]?|100)$"></knowledge-confidence>
    <knowledge-status required enum="pending active completed rejected"></knowledge-status>
    <knowledge-prompt></knowledge-prompt>
    <knowledge-detail></knowledge-detail>
  </knowledge-goal>
</template>

The generic validator

Given a type's <template> element and a real instance element, reads the vocabulary above straight out of the template's own content and performs the same four checks every hand-written check() function in this project used to write by hand: required-and-non-empty, pattern, enum, and unexpected/empty-optional fields. A <template>'s children live in .content, a separate inert DocumentFragment — reading a field's attributes goes through templateEl.content, not the template element directly (verified against happy-dom, the DOM engine this project runs on).

Checking order: schema first, hand-written validator second

A type may still declare its own <script data-validates> alongside its <template>, for logic this vocabulary genuinely can't express. When one exists, the crawler runs the generic check above first, then the hand-written one, and a node is only valid if both pass — the hand-written script is additional validation layered on top of the schema, never a replacement for it. None of this project's seven existing types need one any more; see the decision record.
